skill.name: Fix punctuation in a draft
skill.why: Broken punctuation makes readers stumble, even when the words are great.
skill.how: Read each sentence slowly. Check the ending, the capital, then apostrophes and commas.

steps.say: Let's edit my cafe menu. First, check how each sentence ends. Is it telling or asking?

show.nudge: 'It is made from fish' tells you something, so a full stop is right.
'Do you want a bowl' asks, and it has a question mark. That's right.

steps.ask: Tap the sentence with the wrong end mark.
steps.win: Yes! 'Who wants soup' asks something, so it needs a question mark, not a full stop.

steps.say: Next, check the start. Every sentence starts with a capital letter, and so does every name.

show.nudge: It starts with a capital T and ends with a full stop. It's fine.
Gus is a name, and it starts with a capital. It's fine.

steps.ask: Tap the sentence that needs a capital.
steps.win: Yes! Then starts a new sentence, so it needs a capital T.

steps.say: Now the tricky pair: its and it's. My trick: say 'it is' instead. Does it still work?
steps.ask: Which word goes in the gap?

options.text: Its
options.reason: Say 'it is' instead: 'It is hot in this kitchen!' That works, so it needs the apostrophe.

options.text: It's
Its'
options.reason: No word looks like that. Say 'it is' in the gap. Does it work?

steps.win: Yes! 'It is hot' works, so write it's. It's a short form, and the apostrophe marks the missing i.

steps.say: Careful! Owners usually get an apostrophe, like Mo's soup. But the word its is different.
steps.ask: Which word goes in the gap?

options.text: its
it's
options.reason: Say 'it is': 'The volcano lost it is top.' That's silly, so no apostrophe.

options.text: its'
options.reason: No word looks like that. The top belongs to the volcano. Try 'it is' first.

steps.win: Yes! Its means 'belongs to it', and it never has an apostrophe. Only 'it is' becomes it's.

steps.say: Extra detail can sit in the middle of a sentence. Try covering each part up.

show.nudge: Krak is who roared. Cover that, and we don't know who!
That's what Krak did. Cover it, and the sentence breaks.

steps.ask: Tap the part you could cover up, and the sentence still works.
steps.win: Yes! 'Who was covered in ink' is extra detail about Krak. It sits between two commas.

steps.say: Gus wrote this and forgot one comma. Lots of writers do. Cover the extra detail.

show.text: Gus, the slime expert ate the slime.

options.text: Gus the slime expert, ate the slime.
options.reason: Now the first comma is missing. Extra detail needs a comma on each side.

options.text: Gus, the slime, expert ate the slime.
options.reason: The commas must go around all of the extra detail: the slime expert.

options.text: Gus, the slime expert, ate the slime.

steps.win: Yes! A comma on both sides. Cover the detail, and 'Gus ate the slime' still works.

steps.say: Last, speech. Wren's sentence is split in two by 'said Wren'. Each half needs its marks.

show.text: “Hurry up Gus” said Wren “or we'll miss the boat.”

options.text: “Hurry up Gus,” said Wren, “or we'll miss the boat.”
options.reason: Wren is talking to Gus. Put a comma before his name: Hurry up, Gus.

options.text: “Hurry up, Gus,” said Wren, “or we'll miss the boat.”
“Hurry up, Gus,” said Wren, “Or we'll miss the boat.”
options.reason: Her sentence keeps going after 'said Wren', so or keeps a small letter.

options.text: “Hurry up, Gus” said Wren “or we'll miss the boat.”
options.reason: Check both sides of 'said Wren'. Each side needs a comma.

steps.win: Yes! It's one sentence split in two. Commas on both sides of 'said Wren', and no new capital.

terms.means: A full stop for telling. A question mark for asking.
Starts every sentence and every name.
Say 'it is'. If it works, write it's. If not, write its.
You can cover it up. It needs a comma on both sides.
One spoken sentence cut in two. Commas on both sides, no new capital.

examples.text: “Hurry up, Gus,” said Wren, “or we'll miss the boat.”

card.test: End mark? Capital? Its or it's? Commas on both sides of extra detail and split speech.
